articles.title: Secret Service arrests armed Venezuelan migrant near White House over alleged Trump assassination threat
articles.summary: Secret Service officers arrested a Venezuelan migrant in Washington, D.C., after finding guns in a stolen vehicle and hearing an alleged threat against President Donald Trump.
articles.body: An illegal immigrant from Venezuela was arrested near the White House Thursday after he was allegedly found inside a stolen vehicle carrying multiple guns and reportedly threatening to kill President Donald Trump, according to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). U.S. Secret Service officers approached the suspect Thursday evening after spotting him "acting suspicious in his car while it was parked on Constitution Avenue in Washington, D.C.," DHS told Fox News. The suspect told officers he had heard voices in his head telling him to travel to the nation's capital and kill Trump, DHS said. Officers subsequently learned that the vehicle had been reported stolen, and the suspect admitted to having weapons inside, according to DHS. CAR RAMS INTO WHITE HOUSE BARRICADE, SUSPECT ARRESTED: OFFICIALS A search of the vehicle reportedly turned up three guns, including an AR-15-style rifle and two handguns, along with dozens of rounds of ammunition. The suspect was identified as Ronny Yordrix Guanipa Chrinos, who illegally entered the country through Texas in March 2024 and was subsequently arrested by U.S. Border Patrol, according to officials. He was later released into the country under the Biden administration, authorities said. After his arrest, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) lodged a detainer for Chrinos with the U.S. Marshals Service, which currently has custody of Chrinos. The U.S. Secret Service said the incident reflects a growing threat posed by armed individuals "drawn to the White House complex." "This is the latest example of Secret Service personnel relying on extensive training and experience to de-escalate a volatile situation that posed an imminent threat to our protectees and other Americans," U.S. Secret Service Director Sean Curran said in a statement. "While our personnel are trained to respond to situations like this, and we remain confident in our tactics, we are alarmed by the increase in threat cases that continue to arise." To disrupt threats before they arrive in Washington, Curran said the agency will continue to "focus on proactively investigating and identifying individuals" who raise suspicion. SECRET SERVICE DETAINS, QUESTIONS INDIVIDUAL WHO DROVE VEHICLE INTO BARRICADE NEAR WHITE HOUSE DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin also commended the Secret Service for intervening before the suspect could harm anyone. "This is just an example of the incredible work done by the men and women of the Secret Service every single day as they put their lives on the line to protect our nation’s leaders," Mullin said in a statement. Chrinos was charged with carrying a rifle outside a home or business, three counts of unlawful transportation of a firearm, three counts of possessing an unregistered firearm, three counts of possessing unregistered ammunition, possession of certain dangerous weapons, carrying a pistol without a license, unauthorized use of a motor vehicle, theft and receiving stolen property. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The latest incident comes amid a series of alarming encounters and security breaches near the nation's capital. Just three months ago, a California resident was found near Capitol Hill after driving cross-country with an operational 10-foot guillotine in his pickup truck. He was identified as Philan-Tam-Duy Le. In two separate but similar incidents, suspects also rammed vehicles into security barricades near the White House in March 2026 and October 2025.

articles.title: What are the recount rules in tight Mississippi Senate race?
articles.summary: Lawyers for both campaigns in Mississippi's US Senate race are preparing for a possible legal battle as the close count continues.
articles.body:
The Democrats hold a narrow lead over the Republicans in the US Senate race in Mississippi, with both sides in a dispute over the counting of the remaining votes which could decide the outcome.

Lawyers for each campaign are preparing for a possible legal battle over the final results and weighing in on the examination of ballots.

The result could mark the end of almost 40 years of Republican control over Mississippi's senate seats and will determine the size of the Democrats' majority in the upper house.

Mississippi is the only US state which does not have a set procedure in place to trigger a recount - and the pressure is on to declare a winner with the state's 13 November deadline for certification approaching.

With 97% of the votes counted as of Friday, Democratic candidate Scott Colom is about 2,500 votes ahead of the incumbent Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith.

Mississippi's Secretary of State Michael Watson said on Wednesday that 3,600 "absentee-by-mail ballots" were still to be counted. The state can accept these votes so long as they were postmarked by election day and are received by 10 November.

Watson said there are also an "unknown" number of provisional ballots, also known as affidavit ballots, to be counted. These are typically cast when a voter lacked the required identification to cast their vote. The deadline for voters to resolve any ID issues with provisional ballots, usually by providing acceptable photo identification, is also 10 November.

Mississippi Republican Party Chair Michael Hurst said on Thursday that they estimated there could be "approximately 20,000 outstanding ballots left to be counted".

Hyde-Smith's campaign said the same day that "thousands of votes remain to be counted from dozens of Republican counties" and it is "confident" this will secure her re-election. She has held the seat since 2018.

Colom said the election saw "historic voter turnout" and he is "confident that when votes are counted, we will flip this seat". If he wins, he would be the first black US senator elected in the state since 1875.

What have the campaign lawyers requested?

Colom said his campaign has an "an army of lawyers" ready to act - while the state Republican party said it has sent more than 50 volunteers, attorneys and observers across the state.

Lawyers from both campaigns have sent letters to Mississippi election officials about the counting of outstanding provisional ballots.

The Hyde-Smith campaign lawyers have requested that all 82 counties in the state keep all provisional ballots separate from regular or absentee ballots.

Their letter also requested that election officials preserve various records - including information on how the votes were processed - associated with the provisional ballots as "potential evidence" in a possible legal dispute.

The Colom campaign lawyers responded saying the move has "no legal authority whatsoever".

"Mississippi law does give any candidate a right to examine ballot boxes and their contents within 12 days after the relevant canvass and examination," says Ronald Rychlak, a law professor at the University of Mississippi. "Mississippi's affidavit-ballot statute also requires eligibility review and records concerning whether affidavit ballots were counted."

"Neither law, however, establishes a blanket requirement to segregate all affidavit ballots after they have been accepted," he adds.

The Colom campaign has said the request from Hyde-Smith's team could allow "a particular ballot to be traced to a particular voter", in violation of ballot secrecy laws.

"That's where he does have a more reasonable argument," says Rychlak, "as ballots in the US are private by law and when there's no clear procedure in place there could be a possibility a voter's privacy might be breached."

However, in many states automatic recounts are triggered if a vote is very close, and in others there is an official process for campaigns to request one in a tight race.

Two states, Illinois and Tennessee, allow recounts if a candidate mounts a formal legal challenge.

Mississippi doesn't have a set procedure in place which allows for a result to be automatically recounted even if it's tight or contested.

It is effectively left up to judges in the state to decide how specific disputes should be resolved.

"Mississippi's lack of a formal recount procedure does not leave either campaign without a possible avenue to challenge the result," says Rychlak, "Ballot-box examination is an available post-election mechanism, and that can lead to discoveries that may result in a recount."

There could also be a legal challenge raised at a federal level - with the US Senate potentially having authority to determine who is entitled to the seat.

This would fall under Article I of the US Constitution as there is a provision which gives each chamber of Congress the power to be the "judge of the elections, returns and qualifications of its own members".

articles.title: In 1901, James Atchley homesteaded land in Idaho’s Teton Valley; 125 years later, his descendants have permanently protected 1,686 acres of their potato ranch, which sits on a mule deer migration route from Wyoming
articles.summary: A family ranch near Ashton, Idaho, is now permanently protected by a conservation easement that limits how the land can be developed.
articles.body: A family ranch near Ashton, Idaho, is now permanently protected by a conservation easement that limits how the land can be developed. The agreement safeguards 1,686 acres of Flying A Ranch while allowing the Atchley family to continue farming and ranching. The move also protects an important wildlife migration corridor used by mule deer travelling from Wyoming into Idaho, along with habitat for several other species.A homestead that turned into a potato businessThe Atchley family has worked this land since 1901, when James Arthur Atchley moved from Tennessee and claimed it. He founded Atchley Farms in 1906. According to earlier records, the family’s potato-growing history goes back even further, Teton Valley News reported. In 1923, James won a blue ribbon at the Eastern Idaho State Fair.Today, the ranch covers roughly 5,000 acres and grows seed potatoes on 800 to 1,000 acres. It sells up to 250,000 sacks a year, mostly to buyers in the Pacific Northwest who turn them into French fries, according to the Ashton Chamber of Commerce.The man who pushed for the conservation easementJames Arthur Atchley’s grandson, Clen Atchley, who served on the Teton Regional Land Trust’s (TRLT) early board, was particularly keen to protect the ranch.In an earlier interview with the Wyoming Migration Initiative, Clen explained his reasons. “We realize in watching what’s happening in this county and Teton County that this land is getting to be more valuable, and it’s starting to disappear because they’re developing a lot of it. And we don’t want to see this developed.”He spent years arguing for the protection of eastern Idaho farmland and died in 2024, partway through the project. His daughter, Laura Pickard, and her husband, Clay, now run the ranch day to day. They wanted to honour the family’s legacy and fulfil both Clen’s and James’s wishes. Clen’s widow, Emma Atchley, continued working in the seed potato greenhouse, while the Pickards managed the ranch.“This has been a multiyear project that has come to fruition through countless hours and significant effort... We are so grateful to have been able to work with them to protect this very special part of our farm for many generations to come,” the Pickards said in a statement.A deer route that needed protectionThrough this easement, the Atchley family is protecting not only the ranch but also a deer migration route. Mule deer travel through this landscape from Wyoming and cross into Idaho. Once they cross the border, they depend almost entirely on private land to complete their journey, according to TRLT. Protecting working ranches like this one keeps the route open as development expands elsewhere.“The Flying A property is an exceptional asset within this landscape, supporting a rich assemblage of wildlife species, including many classified as Species of Greatest Conservation Need,” Josh Rydalch, a regional wildlife biologist with the Idaho Department of Fish and Game, said.About 1.3 miles of Bitch Creek runs along the southern edge of the property, supporting streamside habitat.Beyond the ranch, the easement also covers habitat identified as a conservation priority in the Idaho State Wildlife Action Plan, including areas important to grizzly bears, Yellowstone cutthroat trout and ferruginous hawks. The property lies next to two existing TRLT easements, while nearby land is managed by state and federal agencies. Drivers on Idaho State Highway 32 will continue to enjoy views of open farmland.With this easement, the land is protected while remaining in the family’s ownership. The family can continue farming and ranching, as the easement limits development without taking the property away from them. This means the land will not be turned into data centres, residential buildings or similar developments. The project was funded through the family’s donation of the easement, along with support from federal and state programmes and private organisations, including the Knobloch Family Foundation and The Nature Conservancy in Idaho.You use AI every day. articles.title: Cornell faculty pass no-confidence vote over leadership's handling of Jane Doe allegations
articles.summary: Friday's resolution by academic staff is largely symbolic as they do not have the power to remove those in charge of the university.
articles.body:
Cornell University's academic staff have passed a vote of no confidence over its leadership's handling of what staff call a "crisis of sexual assault" after a former student alleged she was gang raped while attending.

The woman, known anonymously as Jane Doe, is suing her former university and the fraternity over an alleged incident involving several men at the Chi Phi fraternity house in October 2024.

All seven of the accused have denied wrongdoing when contacted by the BBC's US partner CBS. None has been charged with a crime.

Friday's no-confidence vote passed by 75 votes to 50. It is largely symbolic because the faculty senate does not have the power to remove leaders.

The resolution states that the faculty senate, which represents academic staff, "has no confidence in the ability of the central administration to effectively address the ongoing crisis of sexual assault at Cornell University".

It did not make any specific recommendations or suggest what administrators did wrong in response to the accusation.

It is a rebuke of university leaders including President Michael Kotlikoff, whom Doe has accused of asking why she waited several weeks to report the incident.

The Ivy League institution in upstate New York has said her account of Kotlikoff's reaction is "incorrect".

Doe's lawyer, Thomas Giuffra, responded to the vote's outcome in a statement, saying: "We recently learned that Cornell's Faculty Senate made a finding of no confidence in the Central Administration's ability to address the longstanding crisis of sexual assault at Cornell.

"We believe that the Faculty Senate did not reach this decision lightly and considered all available information."

Giuffra added: "We are hopeful that this will be yet another step forward to educate and support the Cornell community by addressing the longstanding scourge of sexual assault on campus."

The board of trustees, which does have the power to fire Kotlikoff, said in a statement that it "remains confident" that he and his administration "are the right leaders to thoughtfully and comprehensively address the serious problem of sexual assault on our campus".

Trustees board chairwoman Anne Meinig Smalling, added: "This confidence is rooted not only in the administration's actions to date and plans moving forward, but also in its track record of navigating complex problems."

She also said that the vote of no confidence "reflects the deep anger across our campus and sends a clear signal that what happened to Jane Doe is unacceptable".

Backlash against Cornell has been intense since Doe filed her lawsuit in September. She reported the alleged assault to campus police after it happened but the local prosecutor declined to bring charges at the time.

Cornell, after initially defending its disciplinary measures, has acknowledged it fell short in its handling of her case and has hired a former attorney general to conduct an independent review of the case. It also recently announced a series of measures due assault, including cancelling fraternity parties.

New York state prosecutors, led by Attorney General Letitia James, are carrying out their own investigation to decide if criminal charges are warranted.

Earlier this week, New York Governor Kathy Hochul announced that state police would investigate any future sexual offence complaints at the university.

articles.title: California condo neighbours fought for nearly a decade over a single garage parking space; the winner secured legal ownership, but a court rejected its demand to recover $292,544 in lawyers’ fees
articles.summary: A dispute over a single parking space in an Orange County condominium complex has ended with a clear legal winner and an unusually expensive lesson.
articles.body: A dispute over a single parking space in an Orange County condominium complex has ended with a clear legal winner and an unusually expensive lesson. WCST Enterprises, the owner of Unit 38, successfully proved that it owned garage space 38G-a, the half of a two-car garage that its neighbour Berit Ling had used for roughly two decades. Yet the California Court of Appeal affirmed a ruling that WCST could not recover the $292,544 in attorney fees it sought after winning the case, reported Laws.com and Justia U.S. Law.The decision, issued on September 28, 2026, in WCST Enterprises, LLC v. Ling, is about far more than one inconveniently numbered garage bay. It explains that winning a property dispute does not automatically make the losing neighbour responsible for the winner’s legal costs. In California, a party must still identify a statute or contract that authorises a fee award, and the court found that WCST had not done so.The case began with documents recorded in the 1960s and grew into three appeals, two trials and a fight that consumed nearly ten years. By the end, WCST had secured legal ownership of the space but was left to pay its own lawyers. Read more about it here, as per the reports:One space, two neighboursThe dispute involved adjoining Units 38 and 39 in a condominium complex developed by Huntington Harbor Corporation in the 1960s. WCST, an entity owned by Maury Loomis, bought Unit 38 in 2018. Ling had owned neighbouring Unit 39 since 1998 and had used both halves of the nearby two-car garage, spaces 38G-a and 39G-a, after purchasing her home.The problem was that the recorded documents did not line up neatly with the way residents had used the garages. Ling’s deed referred simply to “39G,” a designation the court found did not actually exist on the complex map. By contrast, WCST’s deed expressly identified garage spaces 38G-a and 38G-b as belonging with Unit 38.WCST knew about the disagreement before it bought the property. The court record states that the sale disclosures told WCST that Unit 39 had been using the entire two-car garage and that litigation to quiet title to space 38G-a might be necessary. Even so, WCST went ahead with the purchase and filed suit against Ling in January 2019.A case that took three appealsWCST initially sued for ejectment, quiet title, violation of the condominium’s covenants, conditions and restrictions, and trespass. After the first trial in 2020, the trial court ruled for Ling. The Court of Appeal reversed that result because the earlier judge’s decision did not adequately explain why Ling had superior rights to the disputed space.The case then went to a new judge for a fresh trial. This time, the court focused first on the quiet title claim and concluded that the garage spaces were privately owned property rather than common areas. It found that WCST’s grant deed clearly conveyed spaces 38G-a and 38G-b with Unit 38, while Ling’s deed referred to a garage designation that could not be located on the plan.After winning on title, WCST waived its remaining claims, including its claim that Ling had violated the CC&Rs. The trial court entered judgment in WCST’s favour, declared it the prevailing party and said attorney fees could be sought by motion. That wording later became central to the fee fight.Why the fee request failedWCST asked for $292,544 in attorney fees under two theories. It relied on Civil Code section 5975, part of California’s Davis-Stirling Common Interest Development Act, and on a fee provision in the complex’s CC&Rs. Both routes require more than simply winning a case involving condominium property.Section 5975 allows a prevailing party to recover reasonable attorney fees and costs in an action to enforce governing documents, such as CC&Rs, bylaws, operating rules and articles of incorporation. The appellate court held that WCST’s lawsuit did not qualify because its core purpose was to enforce rights created by its grant deed, not rights created by the CC&Rs or another governing document.The court explained that it was not enough for a lawsuit to relate to the governing documents. The essential nature of the case had to be enforcement of a specific right those documents provide. Although WCST placed the CC&Rs, the recorded plan and the map into evidence, the court said that merely using documents as exhibits did not transform a deed-based title case into a CC&R enforcement case.“Prevailing party” is not a magic phraseWCST argued that the judgment itself settled the fee question because it called WCST the prevailing party and stated that fees could be recovered through an appropriate motion. The appellate court rejected that argument in plain terms. It said the phrase “prevailing party” is not a “magic incantation” that allows a winner to bypass California’s general rule that each side pays its own attorney fees unless a statute or contract says otherwise.The court also noted that WCST had waived its separate CC&R claim after prevailing on quiet title. The two CC&R provisions WCST later pointed to, involving compliance with covenants and nuisance activity, were part of the claim it abandoned. The court found no evidence that those provisions were actually litigated or that they formed the basis of the quiet title victory.That distinction mattered because other parking disputes have supported fee awards when they involved a specific CC&R provision. The opinion cited Crestmar Owners Assn. v. Stapakis, which concerned a CC&R rule on parking-space transfers, as an example of a case that did qualify for fees under the statute.A costly victoryThe outcome leaves WCST with legal ownership of garage space 38G-a but no reimbursement for the enormous cost of obtaining it. Ling, meanwhile, lost the space she had used for many years, but avoided being ordered to pay WCST’s legal fees. The appellate court also awarded Ling her costs on appeal.For condominium owners, the case is a reminder that property boundaries, deed descriptions and parking assignments can create disputes that last far longer than anyone expects. It also shows why the way a lawsuit is framed can matter as much as the underlying facts. A claim based on a deed may succeed on ownership but offer no route to legal fees, while a properly pleaded claim to enforce a specific CC&R provision may carry fee consequences for either side.In the end, the court’s message was straightforward. WCST proved it owned the space. But proving ownership was not the same as proving that its opponent had to fund the decade-long legal campaign used to establish it.You use AI every day. articles.title: Pyre: Indian film on elderly couple's love and loneliness won 18 awards - now it's wowing audiences
articles.summary: Extraordinary scenes of audiences crying leaving theatres after watching the film have been shared on social media.
articles.body:
A film about the tender love and quiet loneliness of an elderly couple, which took two years to reach cinemas after it was completed, is wowing critics and audiences across India.

The 111-minute Pyre, directed by television journalist-turned-filmmaker Vinod Kapri, also explores the pressing issue of outmigration which has left hundreds of picturesque Himalayan hamlets abandoned and turned them into ghost villages. It further reflects on the impact of climate change, which has made the region's weather increasingly harsh.

On social media, many Indians have shared videos showing audiences leaving theatres with tears in their eyes. Others have posted that they have not been so moved by a film in a long time.

The film's lead actors, ordinary villagers who had never faced a camera before, have also won praise from some of Bollywood's most respected figures, including Naseeruddin Shah and Anupam Kher.

Pyre's protagonists - Padam Singh (played by Kapri's uncle, Padam Singh) and Tulsi (played by Heera Devi) - are Bubu and Aama, local terms for grandfather and grandmother. The couple live in a small home in the mountains of the northern state of Uttarakhand .

It's a place where age is measured against momentous events. Singh was born two years before the outbreak of World War II. Tulsi was born in the year atomic bombs were dropped on Japan.

There are no roads and no electricity. Whenever the couple need help – which is often as Tulsi frequently has to be carried to hospital – Padam Singh uses a traditional long-horn instrument to summon neighbours. In return for their kindness, he pays them with goats.

"There's nothing here – just mountains," as one character puts it. So the young leave in search of greener pastures, and those who depart this beautiful, but blighted, land rarely return.

Kapri says his film remains focused on the "soulful love story of the ageing couple in their last days".

"They have shared a life together for 65 years and, for the last 28 years, they've been waiting for their son, Hariya, who's gone to Mumbai in search of work, to come back," Kapri tells the BBC. "It's a story of companionship, of loneliness and of waiting."

Their wait takes on a new urgency when suddenly, after all these years, a letter arrives from Hariya setting a date for his visit.

As Padam Singh and Tulsi count down the days, the handful of villagers around them leave one by one, until the couple find themselves alone in the vast mountain landscape.

"You and Tulsi should also leave as soon as possible. Otherwise, you won't even have four people to carry your body down the mountain to the funeral pyre when you or Tulsi die," one departing villager advises Padam Singh. "Or die before we leave," he adds in jest.

With no one left to call for help, Padam Singh builds two funeral pyres side by side right outside his door – one for his wife and one for himself.

"How will I carry you down the mountain if you die?" he tells Tulsi when she questions the decision.

Despite the bleak setting and the weight of the topics covered, Pyre is suffused with humour. The central couple are delightful. Like many long-married spouses, they seem to treat bickering as a love language.

Kapri, who is from Uttarakhand, got the idea for the film in 2018 after meeting an 84-year-old man in Munsiyari, a scenic hill town in the state.

"I visited him after seeing his photo in a Facebook post. The wrinkles on his face really fascinated me. His face was unique."

Kapri said he asked him and his wife what their biggest worry was.

"He said, 'My biggest worry is, if I die first, who is going to take care of her?' And she said, 'He doesn't know how to cook. So if I die first, I don't know who is going to cook food for him.' That was so heartwarming for me."

Kapri says he initially tried to make his film with "the real couple", but abandoned the idea after a week of shooting, when it became clear it was not working. He then approached actors Naseeruddin Shah and Ratna Pathak - a couple themselves - for the lead roles.

Shah loved the script, Kapri says, but felt that he and Pathak did not belong to the region and would struggle to do justice to the characters.

Kapri finally found his Padam Singh within his own family – his father's younger brother, a retired army soldier who expressed an interest in acting. He found his Tulsi in another village. Heera Devi, an elderly widow, had raised her children through years of farming, cutting grass and tending to her buffalo.

Over the years, Padam Singh and Heera Devi tell the BBC, they have watched stories of ghost villages, of children migrating for work, abandoning the elderly, play out all around them. They say today they are overwhelmed by the attention Pyre has got.

Since 2024, the film has been screened at some of the world's biggest festivals. It has won 18 awards, Kapri says, including three for best feature and 12 audience-choice best film prizes.

Despite its success at festivals, Kapri says, Pyre spent two years without a distributor. Even OTT platforms passed on the film and it finally reached cinemas only when a producer friend of his stepped in to fund a theatrical release.

But, he says, the modest 70-screen release on 30 October sparked favourable word-of-mouth reviews and with the demand for tickets going up, there was an increase in overall screenings too.

Meanwhile, the misgivings that both Padam Singh and Heera Devi say they initially had about stepping in front of the camera and forgetting their lines are gone now.

Heera Devi says she was even concerned about what her children would think - and what would society say?

Today she and Padam Singh are basking in the positive reviews of film critics and the affection of their audiences.

They have met teary-eyed people at multiple screenings - many wanting to touch their feet and hug them, many who said the film reminded them of their own parents and grandparents who are waiting in villages, towns and cities that they had come from.

"We felt immense joy and happiness. We've received so much love and inspiration - something we had never imagined," says Padam Singh.

But the best moment for him came when he met Naseeruddin Shah in Mumbai. "He watched the entire movie and had tears in his eyes. He hugged me. He said, 'Bubu, the role you have performed, I wouldn't be able to pull off even in seven lifetimes.'"

The film's appeal, Heera Devi says, is because "in reality, our village is just like this".

"Across villages in India, the elderly are left alone. No one's children stay at home anymore and it's the same situation for all parents. They keep waiting for their son and daughter-in-law, hoping that their grandchildren would visit and spend a few days with them. The loneliness is simply unbearable."

Padam Singh says he has a message for the younger generation in Uttarakhand and the rest of India.

"I want to tell them they must not abandon their motherland, the land where they were born," he says. "I also appeal to the government to bring education and employment to where people are - so that they don't have to wander away. When that happens, the parents who are being left behind will also be cared for."

articles.title: From youth offender to junior doctor: 'I wrote a plan and stuck to it'
articles.summary: Steven Beattie left Scotland's most violent prison 20 years ago vowing to turn his life around.
articles.body:
Steven Beattie spent his teenage years in and out of Polmont young offenders' institution, once described by a former governor as "the most violent prison in Scotland" .

He was sent there at 16 after drunkenly crashing a stolen car, and returned repeatedly over the next four years as his involvement with gangs and violence grew.

For Steven, the turning point came when he was punished for his part in a fight by being locked up for 23 hours a day and having his TV removed.

"I never really had time to sit down and think where my life was going," he told the BBC's Scotcast podcast.

"When they took my telly, I finally had that opportunity."

He asked himself - if he kept doing what he was doing, where would he be in five years' time?

"If I don't like that destination, I'll have to change it," he says.

Steven admits it wasn't easy for a young offender to start a new life but, after years of effort, he's about to graduate as a junior doctor.

Steven, who is now 37, grew up in the Hillington area of south-west Glasgow.

His father had the degenerative disease Parkinson's, and his mother was diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia as well as cancer, from which she later died.

"I was under a lot of stress at home," says Steven, who was a carer for both his parents.

He left school at 15, and thinks few of his teachers understood how much stress he had been under because he had been "embarrassed" to tell them.

Looking back, he gives himself "a degree of sympathy" that he didn't do so well in school because of what he was dealing with at home.

"A lot of the time I couldn't make school because I was up to three in the morning looking after my parents," he says.

Steven says avoiding gangs was "impossible" where he grew up in the 1990s and early 2000s, as "gang violence was rife".

The threat of a spell in Polmont kept him out of trouble for a while, but once experienced, its deterrent effect disappeared.

He made close friends while inside and, at first, life there wasn't as bad as he had feared. But he struggled to cope with the relentless noise, especially when he was trying to sleep.

"You've got people kicking your doors and constantly shouting and screaming, and people are in there for months and sometimes years," he says.

"You can imagine the effect it has on a developing brain, being in that environment for years at a time."

Eventually, Steven made a decision to change his life and wrote down three things he had to do - leave Glasgow, quit drinking, and stop hanging around people who got into trouble.

When he left Polmont, he thought most employers would find it difficult to trust him, so he started his own personal training business. He is also an award-winning MMA fighter known as 'Doctor Beatdown'.

Working for himself gave him the ability to save up and move out of Glasgow. But his long-term goal was to become a doctor.

He had been inspired by his dad's neurologist, who had noticed how much Steven was able to understand about his father's Parkinson's.

His school grades were not enough to get him into medical school, so he attended an access course at Glasgow Kelvin college to study physiology at the University of Glasgow.

That then got him into medical school, and in June, he'll graduate as a junior doctor. He hopes to specialise in either surgery, neurology or emergency medicine.

Polmont was back in the news last week when it emerged it had recently experienced the worst prison rioting in decades .

Prison officers from four other jails were called in to restore control during the incident, which involved about 30 inmates.

Linda Pollock, chief executive of the Scottish Prison Service (SPS), said it was an example of "bubbling tension" caused by increasing overcrowding.

Steven says overcrowding can add to pressure inside prison.

"Especially in terms of rehabilitation," he says.

"The staff just no longer have the capacity to give attention to individual prisoners."

He says a lack of attention can make inmates feel they're being left behind and unsupported.

Without support they are unlikely to move on with life after prison, he says.

Steven says his teenage experiences have made him more determined to enjoy the chances he has now.

"I think I've got an appreciation for life that a lot of people don't have because I know how bad it can get," he says.

articles.title: OpenAI sued over claim that ChatGPT drafted lethal poisoning plan
articles.summary: James Gates says he started to suspect his wife was trying to poison him after he found a handwritten note with a list of substances and dosage plans,
articles.body: James Gates says he started to suspect his wife was trying to poison him after he found a handwritten note with a list of substances and dosage plans, some of which were labelled "lethal."At the top of the note were additional instructions: "clear all convos" and "log out of chat GPT," according to a lawsuit Gates filed Thursday against OpenAI, the maker of the world's most popular chatbot. Gates claims his wife, Cheryl, consulted ChatGPT frequently while they were having martial troubles and that the chatbot helped her craft a detailed plan on how to kill him.Legal actions have piled up since 2024 accusing OpenAI and other chatbot makers of inflicting mental health harms on users or coaching them to engage in violence, including murder and suicide. In ongoing lawsuits, OpenAI and other companies have defended themselves by arguing that content generated by chatbots is free speech and not subject to product liability laws. They've also denied that the chatbots are directly responsible for crimes committed by users."Safety is a top priority," OpenAI said in a statement. "We banned this user and have provided information to law enforcement as part of their investigation into this case."Cheryl Gates was charged in 2025 with attempted murder and food contamination after her husband reached out to police. But prosecutors dropped the case in April, citing insufficient evidence, according to state court filings in Charlotte, North Carolina. A spokesperson for the Mecklenburg County DA's Office declined to comment. articles.title: EU tells TikTok to fix ‘harmful’ For You feed, threatens fines
articles.summary: TikTok’s algorithm ‘leading users down rabbit holes they cannot easily escape from’, European Commission says.
articles.body:
The European Union has ordered TikTok to change the algorithm powering its For You feed, threatening the social media platform with large fines.

On Friday, Brussels accused TikTok of violating the EU’s Digital Services Act over the “harmful ‘rabbit holes’ effect” by feeding users similar video clips based on what they’ve previously viewed or liked, even if they are “triggering”.

“Every time a user scrolls or likes a video on TikTok, the algorithm serves more of the same, leading users down rabbit holes they cannot easily escape from,” European Commission Executive Vice President Henna Virkkunen, who oversees tech sovereignty, said in a statement.

“Today’s preliminary findings show again that TikTok needs to step up its efforts to protect users’ well-being, including those of minors.”

The algorithm, according to the EU, results in the “endless” exposure of users to “content about sadness, isolation or body image.”

The EU said that although TikTok had made some changes to mitigate the risks highlighted by the commission, the tweaks were not enough.

TikTok rejected the EU’s findings, saying they are “fundamentally inaccurate and distort our platform’s architecture and our commitment to user safety”.

TikTok has “a strong record of protecting our community while giving users direct and intuitive control over their content experience”, a spokesperson for the tech giant said.

Brussels’ fines on the Chinese-owned platform could increase by up to 6 percent, according to regulators, unless the platform resolves the issue. The company will have a chance to respond before the commission issues its final decision.

Recent efforts in countries like France, Spain and England have focused on protecting minors on social media platforms from predatory behaviour, cyberbullying, deteriorating mental health and eating disorders. Several countries introduced social media bans for children below the age of 15.

In February, the EU found that TikTok did not “adequately assess how these addictive features could harm the physical and mental well-being of its users, including minors and vulnerable adults”.

Whereas the EU’s February findings focused on features such as the impact of notifications, Friday’s order went after the algorithm itself, a senior EU official told the AFP news agency.

In July, the bloc accused TikTok of exposing children to risks like cyberbullying and predatory behaviour.

In the same month, Brussels ordered Meta to change Facebook’s and Instagram’s feeds in an investigation into the platforms’ violations of the bloc’s Digital Services Act.

articles.title: New Zealanders head to polls on final day of voting
articles.summary: More than half of New Zealand’s voters cast early ballots in the tightly contested race.
articles.body:
Polls have opened on the final day of voting in New Zealand against a backdrop of concerns over the rising cost of living and the broader state of the economy.

Polling stations opened at 9am on Saturday (20:00 GMT Friday) and close at 7pm (06:00 GMT Saturday).

Voting already began on October 26. More than 1.6 million voters, out of nearly 3.8 million in total, had cast their ballots by the end of Thursday, according to the country’s Electoral Commission.

The country has strict laws banning any talk of politics on election day.

The 19-hour election day blackout, which ends when polling places close on Saturday evening, bars everyone, including political parties, news outlets and social media users, from commenting on likely election outcomes, campaign issues and anything else that might encourage or discourage people from voting in a particular way.

Billboards and advertising must be removed. Bumper stickers, T-shirts and even social media profile pictures are also covered by the law.

Breaches of the law can incur a fine of up to 20,000 New Zealand dollars ($11,000).

Opinion polls ahead of the tightly contested election suggest the governing centre-right National Party and the opposition centre-left Labour Party neck and neck, with neither on course to win enough seats to govern alone.

New Zealand’s Electoral Commission aims to release preliminary results from 95 percent of polling stations by the end of election night on Saturday. A final result, which will reflect ballots cast by New Zealanders abroad, is expected by November 27.

Most parties are campaigning on the economy, but their suggested solutions differ widely.

The National Party is pledging to return the budget to surplus through fiscal discipline while expanding the national pension scheme.

The Labour Party is focusing on the cost of living, promising cheaper healthcare and transport.

Recent polls show no clear winner. A handful of seats either way could decide who governs.

New Zealand holds a general election every three years under a mixed-member proportional system.

Voters do not elect a leader of the country but instead select a local electorate candidate and a political party.

Electorate winners earn a seat in the typically 120-seat parliament, as do the highest-ranked members of the party based on their national party vote.

articles.title: China confirms discussions are underway on a historic Xi-Trump-Putin meeting
articles.summary: WASHINGTON — Beijing has confirmed for the first time that it is discussing a historic meeting between Chinese leader Xi Jinping, U.S.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — Beijing has confirmed for the first time that it is discussing a historic meeting between Chinese leader Xi Jinping, U.S. President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Mao Ning, a spokesperson for the Chinese foreign ministry, said at a press briefing this week in Beijing that China “is in communication with relevant parties regarding a meeting between the three heads of state.” Nothing is set, but the three-leader gathering would take place this month on the sidelines of a regional summit in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen. If it happens, it would be historic. Experts, however, say the three leaders are unlikely to discuss anything substantive because their interests are at odds, but they would gather for a photo, with China carefully choreographing the meeting. “I think it will happen. The question is the format and the content,” said Sun Yun, director of the China program at the Stimson Center. “China wants the image but not the costs.” Beijing is the host of this year’s leaders summit of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, a 21-member grouping that includes the U.S. and Russia. Trump is expected to travel to Shenzhen to meet Xi for the third time this year, maintaining a fragile trade truce that is set to expire in January. In a sign that tensions persist, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer in a Friday video call with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng urged Beijing to take “concrete actions to fully implement its past commitments, particularly as they relate to agricultural purchases, rare earths, and other critical minerals,” according to a statement from Greer’s office. While he’s in China, Trump has said he would be interested in meeting Xi and Putin to discuss nuclear arms controls, though Putin is focused on talking about the war in Ukraine without Kyiv at the table. “Putin has the most to gain from a leaders’ trilateral, and the Russians are clearly behind the push for a meeting, which would be a diplomatic coup,” said Danny Russel, a former senior State Department official who served in former President Barack Obama’s administration. Trump, with his “crush on authoritarian strongmen,” would love the meeting, though he clearly has been warned by his advisers to steer clear of Ukraine as a topic of the discussions, said Russel, who is now a distinguished fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute. Sun of the Stimson Center said Russia would likely use the summit to nudge China and the U.S. closer to Moscow’s positions on Ukraine, while “China will have to manage Russian manipulation.” China also would not engage in talks of arms controls or discussions about Ukraine or Iran, other than its diplomatic refrain that peace is important and wars should end, Sun said. Beijing’s biggest challenge may be the perception. The summit “should not be equated to three great powers dividing up the world,” she said. The meeting may amount to no more than a photo opportunity that would allow Putin to be seen next to U.S. and Chinese leaders, said Craig Singleton, senior director of the China program at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies. “But these photo opportunities have diminishing diplomatic returns,” Singleton said. “The spectacle may be historic without producing anything particularly consequential.”

articles.title: An Australian woman struggled to fund her first camp for children fighting cancer, ending up $300 in debt; but the programme eventually grew into a national charity
articles.summary: An Australian woman who struggled to pay for her first camp for children with cancer ended the event more than $300 in debt, despite giving its young
articles.body: An Australian woman who struggled to pay for her first camp for children with cancer ended the event more than $300 in debt, despite giving its young participants an experience they needed. Vera Entwistle's determination to make childhood more enjoyable for children facing cancer eventually laid the foundations for Camp Quality, a charity that grew from a small gathering in 1983 into a nationwide support organisation. Its early years were marked by financial difficulties but the programme continued to expand, creating opportunities for children and their families to spend time together away from the demands of cancer treatment.How Vera Entwistle turned a $300 debt into Camp QualityAccording to Camp Quality Australia's official history, Entwistle arrived in Australia from the United States in 1983 and began looking for volunteer opportunities supporting children with cancer. She was surprised to discover that no charity in the country offered the kind of support she had hoped to provide, prompting her to establish one herself.Her idea was simple but meaningful. Children dealing with cancer deserved opportunities to enjoy childhood, make friends and participate in activities that were not centred on hospitals or medical treatment.The first attempt was far from easy. When Entwistle approached a hospital in 1983 with her proposal to take children with cancer to a camp, she was initially discouraged and told to find something else to do.However, she refused to abandon the idea. Her determination was strengthened after hearing about a little girl with terminal cancer who had laughed again after going camping. Entwistle wanted other children to experience the same happiness.The first camp faced financial difficulties but succeededCamp Quality Australia records that its inaugural children's camp was held towards the end of 1983. Although Entwistle finished the event more than $300 in debt, it was considered a major success by both her and the children who attended.The camp also attracted encouraging feedback from doctors, who began reporting improvements in the children's wellbeing. Participants were eager to return, providing an early indication that the programme was meeting a genuine need.Entwistle eventually found a hospital willing to support her idea. She was taken to a children's oncology ward, where she asked young patients what they wanted to do during their camp.Children wanted to paddle canoes and try archery, experiences that Entwistle believed could be arranged without difficulty. The response helped shape the programme around what children themselves wanted.A devastating loss did not stop the charity from growingCamp Quality's founder profile states that 37 of the 38 children who attended that initial gathering eventually died.The organisation's Australian history explains that cancer survival rates in 1983 were considerably lower than they are today. Only one child from the first camp survived the disease, making the early years particularly painful for Entwistle and those involved.Despite those losses, the founder remained committed to improving the quality of life for children growing up with cancer.Entwistle received inspiration for the name from a doctor who expressed the idea that although nobody could increase the quantity of another person's life, everyone could improve its quality.That philosophy became central to the charity's work, focusing on happiness, companionship and memorable experiences even when medical outcomes remained uncertain.What helped Camp Quality reach more Australian familiesThe charity's expansion gathered momentum in 1988, when a television crew from Good Morning Australia visited one of its camps. Entwistle subsequently received more than 500 letters from doctors, nurses, children and parents expressing interest in supporting or attending the programme.Support from Ansett Australia, which helped provide free air travel, proved particularly important. It enabled Camp Quality to establish 11 additional camp locations around Australia and introduce Family Camps, allowing parents and other relatives to participate alongside children.From children's camps to a broader support networkEntwistle's work eventually extended beyond organising recreational activities. Camp Quality Australia says that, during her 17 years leading the charity, she and her husband, Brian, developed children's camps, family camps and a school cancer education programme.She also helped communities establish their own versions of Camp Quality, including programmes overseas in Ireland, India and New Zealand.The organisation records another important development in 1989, when its puppet programme was established. Entwistle had spoken with children returning to school after cancer treatment and recognised the need to help classmates understand what they had experienced.Scripts based on children's real-life experiences were developed for the programme. With funding from Paul Newman and Ronald McDonald Children's Charities, the cancer education initiative was subsequently offered free to schools.How Camp Quality became an established charityAfter 17 years leading the organisation, Vera and Brian Entwistle retired in 2000. Their departure marked the beginning of a new phase, with Simon Rountree appointed chief executive.The charity continued adapting its services as the needs of families changed. In 2014, it joined forces with cancer charities Redkite and Canteen to reduce duplication and improve cooperation between organisations.During the Covid-19 pandemic, Camp Quality also developed digital services to reach children who were isolated, living in remote areas or unable to attend in-person activities. Its Australian history records the introduction of online initiatives, virtual camps and digital puppet playdates.By 2023, when the charity celebrated 40 years since its first camp, more than 10,000 children aged up to 15 were registered for its free services and programmes. It also had almost 800 registered volunteers, highlighting the scale of the community that had developed around Entwistle's original idea.The legacy of the first camp extends beyond AustraliaCamp Quality's story also reached New Zealand, where its first camp was held in Auckland in 1985. The event brought together 22 children from across the country.The organisation has since expanded to 5 regions, from the far North to the deep South, providing camps and recreational activities for more than 300 children and young people annually. It describes itself as the only organisation in New Zealand providing camps for children living with cancer.The hot air balloon featured in its logo symbolises the ability to rise above life's challenges, reflecting the philosophy associated with Entwistle's work.You use AI every day. articles.title: Venezuelan man who said voices told him to kill Trump is arrested near White House, DHS says
articles.summary: A Venezuelan man who had guns in his vehicle and told officers that voices in his head urged him to kill President Donald Trump was arrested Thursday near the White House, the federal government said.
articles.body: A Venezuelan man who had guns in his vehicle and told officers that voices in his head urged him to kill President Donald Trump was arrested Thursday near the White House, the federal government said. The Department of Homeland Security said Friday that Ronny Yordrix Guanipa Chrinos was approached by Secret Service officers who alleged he was acting suspiciously while parked on Constitution Avenue. “When they confronted the suspect, he said that he heard voices in his head telling him to come to Washington, D.C. and kill President Trump,” the Department of Homeland Security said in a statement. Chrinos, who federal officials said was in the country illegally, was in a vehicle that had been reported stolen, officials said. He told officers there were weapons inside, and officers then found an AR-15 style rifle, a MAC-10 handgun, a Glock 43X pistol and ammunition, DHS said. A Secret Service police officer affidavit filed in court says that Chrinos, 26, was asleep in a parked blue Ford F-150 when he was awoken and confronted by officers at 11:42 p.m. Thursday. At first, officers treated it as a welfare check, but Chrinos used Google Translate to tell an officer that he had weapons he wanted to turn over to the government, the affidavit says. Chrinos also said through Google Translate: “I have the item they wanted to kill me over, along with the outfit to go with it; if you want, I can hand it over without putting up any resistance,” the affidavit says. According to the court document, he also allegedly said through the app: “I have the gun because they tried to kill me with it, and I had to take it away from them; it’s in the brown bag.” Chrinos told investigators that the truck belonged to his boss, who had lent it to him, the affidavit said. He also said he had bought the weapons a month ago and had been living in the vehicle. Chrinos was charged with carrying a rifle outside a home or business, three counts of unlawful transportation of a firearm, three counts of unregistered firearms and three counts of unregistered ammunition, DHS said. He was also charged with one count each of possession of certain dangerous weapons, carrying a pistol without a license, unauthorized use of a motor vehicle, theft and receiving stolen property, the department said. A federal law enforcement source said that prosecutors are reviewing the evidence against Chrinos and that he will be in federal court on Monday. He was in custody Friday, DHS said. It was not clear whether he had an attorney who could speak on his behalf. DHS said Chrinos entered the U.S. illegally in 2024, was arrested by Border Patrol and later released. DHS did not provide further details about his case. Secret Service Director Sean Curran said the arrest highlights the agents’ training and aim to de-escalte volatile situations. “While our personnel are trained to respond to situations like this and we remain confident in our tactics, we are alarmed by the increase in threat cases that continue to arise,” Curran said in a statement.

articles.title: What happens if the internet goes down? BlackSky - the UK's emergency backup plans
articles.summary: A Black Sky event could leave millions without power, water and communications. So how prepared is the UK?
articles.body:
It was a Saturday night in early December when Roger Kemp realised something was very wrong.

"I was halfway through a Scandi crime drama when everything went off," the professor at Lancaster University told the BBC. "Streetlights were off. The sodium glow that we can see over the horizon from Morecambe was off."

"[It was] almost like a zombie movie," he said. "People trying to find phone reception, wondering where things were, and there was a huge queue at the one working telephone box."

At 22:45 on 5 December 2015, the River Lune - which flows directly through Lancaster - had flooded, and the electricity supply to 61,500 people in the city went.

Households lost light and heat, some water supplies also began to fail because they relied on electric pumps. The railway station closed. So too petrol stations and shops. Most cash machines didn't work. Traffic lights failed.

Responsible or panicked? Meet the people around the world already preparing for crisis

Why should I stockpile and what will I need?

The two communication systems that survived were copper wire landline telephones and FM radio. The local commercial radio station The Bay had an emergency generator and one landline and a reporter was sent outside the affected area to ring in with information.

Three months later, Kemp, a professor of engineering with a specialism in safety and electrical systems, gathered people together to look at everything that had gone wrong.

"It is perhaps ironic that, in a society with huge commitment to digital infrastructure, the most reliable source of news was a commercial station using technology that would have been familiar to the engineers on the 1960s Radio Caroline pirate radio ship," the subsequent report concluded.

For Kemp and others in the field of civil contingency, Lancaster was a warning. When a town loses power for several days, our connected world falls apart. This kind of disruption has been given a name: a Black Sky event.

At a recent summit on UK resilience, the conversation focused on the need for the UK to be able to withstand a Black Sky event for a minimum of 72 hours.

"We are nine meals from anarchy" is a phrase often heard in the civil contingency world. A brutal reminder of the fear that three days without food would be enough to turn a crisis into chaos. If a Black Sky event takes out electricity, water, shops and communications, there is a good reason the government wants us to have our own supplies.

The much talked about "Be Prepared" campaign is designed to help ready us for all sorts of possible crises, but the government says there is no specific threat to the grid. Regardless, a Black Sky event is definitely at the backs of people's minds.

In a major emergency, we are being told to hunker down and turn on an FM radio, as thousands did in Lancaster. This is why the BBC has its own Black Sky plan.

Only a small number of staff know the full details, but from what I have gleaned, about 100 people in the BBC will run a special emergency radio studio.

It will have secure lines of communication not dependent on the internet, and fuel, water and food to ensure it can operate without resupply for at least three days.

This emergency service will broadcast pre-arranged government messaging. The scripts have already been published online.

They include instructions on how much people should be drinking each day and how to dispose of toilet waste without flushing the toilet.

Other information will be broadcast via satellite vehicles from a select number of journalists at emergency centres around the UK, which will carry on as long as the diesel lasts.

The BBC's broadcasts will be sent via radio transmission towers, isolated from the internet and equipped with tanks of between five and 40,000 litres (8,800 gallons) of diesel to keep their generators going for three days - FM radio is power hungry. The teams will be using satellite phones to keep in touch and if these stop working there are pre-agreed protocols and meet-up points.

Why FM? Because it works almost everywhere, even in a blackout or a crippling cyber-attack.

"It was originally thought we should plan for five to seven days," I was told quietly by one BBC insider. "The latest advice from Neso [National Energy System Operator] is that they will probably be able to get the power back on in two to three days."

Of course, fears of a grid failure are not new, but recent events such as the mass blackout in Spain, Portugal and south-western France in April 2025 have pushed it up the agenda. And the more it happens, the more it reveals the problems it can create in our networked world.

People need to know power cuts are about more than just the lights going out, says Lord Harris, chair of the UK's National Preparedness Commission. ''It's likely to stop the water supply because unless you happen to be located neatly downstream of a reservoir, that requires electricity," he told me.

More importantly, sewage tends to solidify unless water can move through it, he adds, "and that then causes blockages, the whole thing backs up, you get sewage flowing out, flowing back up the system".

It's common for governments in Europe to regularly advise households to stock up on supplies in case of a national emergency - but the UK is behind in its warnings to the population.

However, work has begun on some backup systems, such as High Altitude Pseudo-Satellites (HAPS). The government is spending £70m developing planes that can circle over the UK and provide at least a week of emergency mobile phone and internet connectivity at times of crisis.

"When ground networks fail, there are limits to what satellites can provide as a fallback," said Rico Chandra, programme director for Enduring Atmospheric Platforms, the company developing HAPS plans.

We live in a complex, electrically powered world - but the more connected everything becomes the more catastrophic it is when that fails.

In the drive towards efficiency over the last five decades, we've lost backup systems, says Lord Harris.

An example of this is the new communication system being adopted by the emergency services, which will replace radio comms with mobile phone network technology, says Lord Harris, "so if the mobile phone goes down it will also impact on emergency services communications".

However, the government insists "moving emergency services onto modern 4G and 5G technologies" is "resilient and reliable".

Government enthusiasm for resilience is nothing new. Oliver Dowden, the then deputy prime minister, launched the last Conservative government's disaster planning initiative in May 2024. The launch was somewhat overshadowed by Sunak announcing an election on the same day but, two years on, calls for at least three days of resilience have only grown stronger.

At the beginning of researching this article I spoke to an engineer about the UK's TV and radio transmission masts, their lonely isolation from the rest of the digital landscape sounded like a failing. It now feels like an argument in their favour.

The current urgency for disaster planning is coming at an interesting moment for technology we used to rely on. The UK's copper wire landline system - which would work even in a power cut - will be switched off on 31 January 2027. The future of FM radio is also under government review.

The response from the government was that while copper landlines had been a useful fallback during power cuts, they were now unreliable and difficult to repair.

As I ended my call with Kemp, I asked him if his report had helped improve our readiness for a Black Sky. He paused.

"If anything, we've gone backwards," he said. "Switching off the public switch telephone network, I think shows that there has been really no thought at all about how you communicate when you've no longer got power."

While writing this piece last Saturday I had to break off for an hour because my street was suddenly plunged into darkness. We had a power cut.

I found my emergency torch, but the batteries had leaked. My candles had been pushed to the back of a cupboard and I had no idea where I had put my wind-up radio with its emergency torch.

articles.title: SC settles 60-yr Bhakra & Beas dispute between Punjab, Haryana and HP
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: SC Friday approved a cashless settlement chaperoned by attorney general R Venkataramani of a 60-year-old dispute between three states over
articles.body: NEW DELHI: SC Friday approved a cashless settlement chaperoned by attorney general R Venkataramani of a 60-year-old dispute between three states over sharing of electricity generated by Bhakra-Nangal and Beas power projects, and directed Punjab and Haryana to supply 598 million units every year, during Oct-March, to Himachal Pradesh for the next 20 years.Giving effect to a 2011 SC decree in favour of Himachal, the court expressed concern the state had still not received the benefits of a case it filed in 1996, even after 15 years.A bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana said, "As a matter of abundant concern, we must express in no uncertain terms to all stakeholders concerned that the directions issued by this court are binding and are required to be acted upon without reservation."The expectation of decree, having remained pending for several decades, cannot be rendered fruitless by reason of the unwillingness or recalcitrance of a judgement debtor (Punjab and Haryana)," the bench said, adding that the total energy arrears of approximately 11,973 million units are to be supplied to Himachal over the next 20 years.The court also directed that Himachal's liability towards the project cost be adjusted against its pending power share dues.After the adjustment, its entitlement was fixed at 11,973 million units over 20 years, compared with around 13,000 million units before the deduction.On Sept 27, 2011, SC had decreed the suit in favour of Himachal by ruling, "It is hereby declared that the plaintiff-state is entitled to 7.19% of the power of the composite State of Punjab from the Bhakra-Nangal project with effect from Nov 1, 1966, and from Beas project with effect from the dates of production in Unit I and Unit II." articles.title: NYU professor and podcaster calls Elon Musk a 'traitor,' compares him to Soviet spies excuted during Cold War
articles.summary: Scott Galloway compared Elon Musk to Soviet spies who gave away U.S. nuclear secrets on his podcast, calling him a "traitor to the West" over throttling Starlink access in Ukraine.
articles.body: NYU professor and podcaster Scott Galloway called SpaceX CEO Elon Musk a "traitor" Tuesday and compared him to Julius and Ethel Rosenberg. The Rosenbergs were convicted of conspiracy to commit espionage for the Soviet Union in a case involving U.S. atomic secrets and later executed. On Election Day, Galloway laid out an alternate history scenario on his "Prof G Podcast" to draw a comparison between Musk's actions and a hypothetical World War II scenario involving aviator Charles Lindbergh. Galloway was referring to reports that SpaceX restricted Starlink satellite internet speeds in Ukraine last month, reportedly disrupting Ukrainian military operations during the country's war with Russia. "I want to propose a scenario," Galloway said. "It's the '30s, we're contemplating reentering Europe. Paid a huge price in World War I. It's a very unpopular idea to go back where it feels like we just left, and this innovator, Charles Lindbergh, is saying, ‘No, we should partner with the Germans.’ ELON MUSK LANDS NEW TRUMP ADMINISTRATION ROLE SHAPING FUTURE OF AMERICAN WARFARE "Imagine, if you will, that Lindbergh was able to raise a ton of money and buy McDonnell Douglas, an aircraft manufacturer, and put in place this unbelievably innovative guidance system and FDR decided to loan to the RAF (Royal Air Force) B-17s, an amazing bomber in defense of Europe as this fascist begins to invade Europe," he said. "And then the CEO of McDonnell Douglas, Charles Lindbergh, decides mid-flight, to turn off the guidance systems. And, as a result, the blitzkrieg increases in fury and U.K. citizens are killed. "I believe that has almost exactly played out in the last few weeks with Elon Musk throttling back Starlink," Galloway said. "And my question is, or my thesis is, we took the Rosenbergs and put them up against a wall and executed them for being traitors. And I realize this is an incendiary statement, but I'll make it, and I believe it. I think Elon Musk is a traitor to the West." Julius and Ethel Rosenberg were executed in 1953 after being convicted of conspiracy to commit espionage for the Soviet Union in a case involving U.S. atomic secrets. "And I think what is even more dangerous is this zeitgeist within America that the idolatry of innovators and money has created a cloud cover such that traitors to the West are not seen as traitors to the West," Galloway further argued. "That if this had happened in any other age where we were not obsessed with innovators and money, a much different reaction would be playing out for Elon Musk." Musk said Ukraine was using Starlink in violation of the service's restrictions, saying, "Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed." HOW ELON MUSK GOT BACK IN TRUMP'S ORBIT AFTER NUCLEAR FALLOUT, INSIDERS REVEAL: 'WATER UNDER THE BRIDGE' On a recent episode of the "Pivot" podcast with co-host Kara Swisher, Galloway made similar comments, saying, "We lined up the Rosenbergs against a wall. This is a traitor to the West, and he should be held to the same standards as every other traitor in the West." "Comparing Elon Musk to the Rosenbergs is ludicrous," Theo Wold, a former White House deputy assistant for domestic policy during President Donald Trump’s first term, said in a statement to Fox News Digital about Galloway’s rhetoric. "Elon Musk is an innovator who epitomizes the technological advances and optimism that are at the center of Western civilization, which, incidentally, Democrats loved, that is, until Musk exercised his First Amendment freedoms to support Republicans. "That is no crime, and the only thing Scott Galloway is pushing for is a nakedly partisan witch hunt and the endorsement of violence against the Antifa Democrats’ political enemies." articles.title: Meet Pim Neill, the six-year-old Pittsburgh Girl Scout who wanted to sell cookies after watching older girls and sold over 120,000 boxes with viral TikTok videos
articles.summary: Pim Neill, a six-year-old Girl Scout kindergartner from Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, has sold more than 120,000 boxes of Girl Scout cookies in a single
articles.body: Pim Neill, a six-year-old Girl Scout kindergartner from Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, has sold more than 120,000 boxes of Girl Scout cookies in a single season, a record-breaking total driven by viral TikTok videos her father posted. Each clip opened with the same polite question to strangers, and together they drew millions of views and earned her a national appearance on CBS Mornings. Her sales had already broken the Pennsylvania single-season record for Girl Scout cookies before she reached 100,000 boxes. The latest reported count stands at 121,546 boxes, and the total was still climbing when the most recent report was published.How a three-year-old watching older girls at a cookie booth set a Pittsburgh dream in motionHer father, Luke Anorak-Neill, told Pittsburgh Magazine that the story began at a cookie booth inside the David L. Lawrence Convention Centre. There, three-year-old Pim watched older girls selling boxes and decided she wanted to do the same. He told CBS News Pittsburgh that this simple observation made her want to become a Girl Scout, and that it reflects what most people think is the only job of a Girl Scout, selling cookies.Two troops turned her away before a kindergarten-only Girl Scout troop finally welcomed herFinding a troop took longer than the family expected. Anorak-Neill told CBS News Pittsburgh that the first troop they approached said Pim’s disabilities would hold the group back and did not want her to join. A second troop declined because she was too young, and a father there said that little girls rarely show up and leave the older girls to do the work. Anorak-Neill decided those groups did not speak for every troop. The family kept looking and found a kindergarten-only troop in the Baldwin-Whitehall area, which they travelled to from the city of Pittsburgh. He describes the 11 kindergartners as a great fit.A Niagara Falls trip, many specialist visits, and a first week that reached her predicted limitPim’s first target was 2,026 boxes, the Daisy incentive for a trip to Niagara Falls. The place matters to her parents, who visited it early in their relationship. Her local service unit manager told the family that 819 boxes were probably her limit, so she hoped Pim was not too attached to the prize. Pim had 819 boxes sold by the first Friday of the season, which began on 6 January. Pittsburgh Magazine reported that her daily routine helped. According to her father, Pim has several diagnosed conditions, and the family visits roughly a dozen specialists. Cookies were therefore sold in and outside specialist offices and in nearby communities, while neighbourhood group posts, emails and a growing contact list pushed the total up.One short TikTok greeting went viral, and a goal update video sent her sales soaring within a dayEvery Girl Scout gets her own web page for online orders, so Anorak-Neill began posting short videos of Pim on TikTok with a link to hers. Each one began the same way: “Hi, my name is Pim. Do you want to buy some Girl Scout cookies?” The family already had about 1,200 followers from earlier videos of Pim, and as they posted regularly, the clips took off.He said he almost did not post the first one. Pim did not make eye contact and looked to the side while speaking, and he feared the internet would turn on her. Pim told him it was fine and to post it. Viewers rallied around her instead.When she passed 5,000 boxes, her father asked whether she wanted to stop. She chose to carry on, set a goal of 10,000 and later said she wanted to sell more cookies than anyone. Within about 24 hours of the video announcing that goal, she sold more than 20,000 boxes. By mid-February she had passed 81,000, enough to break the Pennsylvania record, and the family’s next target was 100,000.Why her father says Pim is simply a little girl who loves counting, reading and chasing goalsAnorak-Neill rejects the idea that parents are pushing the numbers. He said Pim loves counting and watching numbers rise, and that she showed early signs of pattern recognition. She recognised words before the age of one. Her love of books led her to finish the Mount Lebanon Library’s 1,000 Books Before Kindergarten programme early, and she now logs hundreds of books a year in summer reading contests.He said prizes are not what drives her. In a school fundraiser with no rewards, she still sold a significant share of the items. At church, she collected donation supplies for an animal shelter, and neighbourhood clean-ups at home later counted towards Girl Scout badges. In his view, the organisation’s patches, milestones and visible progress markers suit her mindset. He also said the experience is teaching her hard work, goal setting and how to be an entrepreneur.The attention has had an unexpected effect, Pim is now more willing to talk to customers and appear on camera. In February, she delivered cookies to Pittsburgh’s mayor, Corey O’Connor, who declared 20 February Pim Neill Day. Her father said the sales strategy comes second to her own motivation, and that he reminded himself at every step that the effort should be girl-led, true to the spirit of Girl Scouts. In his words: “This is just a little girl who really likes goals.”You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
